title: Web Crawler
summary: Crawl billions of pages politely: a prioritised URL frontier with per-host queues, robots.txt and rate limits, distributed fetchers, content dedup, and a pipeline that feeds the index.

head: Type
Requirement
rows: Start from seed URLs, fetch pages, extract links, repeat
Store raw HTML (and extracted text) for indexing
Re-crawl pages based on how often they change
Politeness: obey robots.txt; never overload one host
Scale to billions of pages per month; robust to traps and bad HTML
Don't crawl the same URL or near-identical content twice

blocks.text: Bandwidth ~ 400 × 100 KB ≈ 40 MB/s average. The hard part isn't throughput, it's politeness and dedup at billions of URLs.

items: Fetchers take URLs from the frontier, respecting each host's crawl delay.
Raw pages go to blob storage; a message with the location goes to the parser.
The parser extracts links, normalises them, drops ones already seen, and enqueues the rest with a priority.

sections.title: Deep dive: the URL frontier and politeness

items.title: Front queues (priority)
items.text: Score URLs by PageRank-ish importance, freshness need, and depth; higher-priority queues are drained more often.

items.title: Router
items.text: Hash the host to one of many back queues, so every host lives in exactly one queue.

items.title: Back queues (politeness)
items.text: Each back queue is served by one worker at a time; a heap of (next_allowed_time, queue) enforces per-host delay.

items.title: Re-crawl
items.text: Pages that changed on the last visit get re-scheduled sooner; static pages decay to weeks.

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: Politeness is enforced structurally: one queue per host, one in-flight request per host, and a min-heap of next allowed fetch times. That's the classic Mercator frontier design.

items: **URL dedup:** normalise (lowercase host, strip fragments, sort query params), then check a seen-set. At billions of URLs a **Bloom filter** in memory gives a fast "definitely new" answer; a false positive only means skipping one URL.
**Content dedup:** hash the page body for exact duplicates; use **SimHash** / MinHash fingerprints for near-duplicates (mirrors, boilerplate changes).
**Crawler traps:** infinite calendars and session-id URLs — cap depth and URL length, cap pages per host, and detect repeating path patterns.
**DNS:** cache aggressively; DNS lookups are a surprising bottleneck at crawl scale.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Keeping the seen-URL set in a SQL table and querying it per link. With ~50 links per page and thousands of pages per second that's 100k+ lookups/s — use an in-memory probabilistic filter backed by a sharded KV store.

items: Partition the frontier and seen-set by host hash, so a worker owns whole hosts — politeness stays local, no global coordination.
Checkpoint frontier state; a crashed worker's hosts are reassigned and resumed.
Timeouts and size limits on fetches; treat slow hosts as lower priority.
Handle JavaScript-heavy sites with a separate, much more expensive headless-browser rendering tier.

cols.title: BFS from seeds
cons: Hammers popular hosts without a politeness layer

cols.title: Prioritised frontier
pros: Spends budget on valuable / changing pages
cons: Needs scoring signals and more state

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: The frontier is two-level: priority queues decide what to crawl, per-host queues decide when. Dedup is a Bloom filter for URLs and fingerprints for content.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Scale, freshness, HTML only or rendering, politeness rules.

items.title: HLD
items.text: Frontier → fetchers → store → parser → dedup → frontier.

items.title: Deep dives
items.text: Politeness queues, Bloom filter, SimHash, traps.

items.title: Scale
items.text: Partition by host, checkpoints, rendering tier.

items.q: How do you decide re-crawl frequency?
items.a: Track change rate per page (hash differs between visits) and schedule proportionally, bounded by importance.

items.q: How do you crawl only part of the web, e.g. news?
items.a: Seed with news sites and sitemaps, and score URLs by topic/host allow-lists.

items.q: What if a host's robots.txt changes?
items.a: Cache it with a TTL (e.g. 24 h) and re-fetch; treat fetch failure conservatively.

items.q: How big is the Bloom filter for 10B URLs at 1% FP?
items.a: About 9.6 bits per element → ~12 GB, shardable across machines.

items: Frontier = priority queues + per-host back queues + next-fetch heap.
Normalise URLs; Bloom filter for seen-set.
Cap depth/pages per host to escape traps.
